raw_text:
# Sacubitril/Valsartan (Angiotensin Receptor-Neprilysin Inhibition) in Heart Failure: A Narrative Review

Heart failure (HF) remains a major global public health concern characterized by high morbidity, mortality, and impaired quality of life. For decades, therapeutic strategies focused solely on suppressing the overactive renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) and the sympathetic nervous system. The introduction of sacubitril/valsartan, a first-in-class angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI), revolutionized the HF treatment landscape by simultaneously blocking the AT1 receptor and enhancing the endogenous natriuretic peptide system [1, 2, 3]. This narrative review summarizes the clinical development, mechanism of action, and therapeutic expansion of sacubitril/valsartan across the heart failure spectrum.

### Mechanism of Action
Neprilysin is a neutral endopeptidase responsible for the degradation of various endogenous vasoactive peptides, including atrial, brain, and C-type natriuretic peptides, bradykinin, and adrenomedullin [3]. By inhibiting neprilysin, sacubitril increases the bioavailability of these peptides, promoting vasodilation, natriuresis, diuresis, and antifibrotic effects [3]. However, neprilysin also degrades angiotensin II; thus, neprilysin inhibition alone would elevate circulating vasoconstrictor levels. Combining sacubitril with the angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB) valsartan counteracts this limitation, ensuring effective blockade of the deleterious effects of angiotensin II on the AT1 receptor [1, 3].

### Heart Failure with Reduced Ejection Fraction (HFrEF)
The therapeutic efficacy of sacubitril/valsartan in chronic HFrEF was established by the landmark PARADIGM-HF trial [1]. This randomized, double-blind study evaluated 8,399 patients with HFrEF (LVEF ≤40%) and demonstrated that sacubitril/valsartan reduced the composite primary endpoint of cardiovascular death or HF hospitalization by 20% compared to the angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor (ACEi) enalapril [1]. Furthermore, ARNI therapy reduced both sudden cardiac death and death due to worsening HF [4], while significantly improving health-related quality of life [5]. Despite these clear advantages, registry data such as the CHAMP-HF study highlighted substantial gaps in real-world implementation, underscoring the need for structured initiation strategies [6].

To address safe titration and outpatient initiation, the TITRATION trial evaluated slow versus rapid up-titration regimens, finding that a more gradual initiation was better tolerated in patients previously on low-dose RAAS inhibitors [7]. This was particularly true when considering baseline hemodynamic parameters like systolic blood pressure [8]. Furthermore, mechanistic trials such as EVALUATE-HF and PROVE-HF provided objective evidence of cardiac reverse remodeling, showing significant reductions in left ventricular volumes, improved ejection fraction, and decreased aortic stiffness [9, 10]. However, in patients with advanced, end-stage chronic HFrEF (NYHA class IV), the LIFE trial demonstrated that sacubitril/valsartan did not offer a superior reduction in N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) or clinical events compared to valsartan alone, pointing to a potential therapeutic ceiling in advanced disease [11].

### Initiation in the Acute Decompensated Setting
While chronic HFrEF was the initial focus, the PIONEER-HF trial expanded the clinical application of sacubitril/valsartan to hospitalized patients stabilized after acute decompensated heart failure (ADHF) [12]. In-hospital initiation of sacubitril/valsartan led to a 29% greater reduction in NT-proBNP at 8 weeks compared to enalapril, accompanied by a significant reduction in rehospitalizations [12]. The TRANSITION study corroborated these findings, proving that initiating ARNI therapy either in-hospital or shortly after discharge was both safe and highly feasible, establishing the early use of sacubitril/valsartan as a key strategy to protect patients during the vulnerable post-discharge period [13].

### Expansion Across the LVEF Spectrum: HFmrEF and HFpEF
Following its success in HFrEF, sacubitril/valsartan was investigated in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF, LVEF ≥45%) in the PARAGON-HF trial [2]. Although sacubitril/valsartan did not achieve statistical significance for the primary composite endpoint of cardiovascular death and total HF hospitalizations compared to valsartan, it showed a strong trend toward benefit (6% relative risk reduction, p=0.059) [2]. Prespecified subgroup analyses revealed significant benefit in patients with LVEF between 45% and 57%, as well as in women [12]. 

In a prespecified pooled analysis of more than 13,000 patients with heart failure enrolled in both PARADIGM-HF and PARAGON-HF, sacubitril/valsartan reduced heart failure hospitalization and cardiovascular death compared with renin-angiotensin-aldosterone–system inhibitors, showing that the greatest therapeutic benefits extend across the mildly reduced ejection fraction (HFmrEF) spectrum up to an LVEF of approximately 55% to 60% [15]. This was further supported by the PARAGLIDE-HF trial, which evaluated patients with LVEF >40% stabilized after a worsening HF event and showed a significant reduction in NT-proBNP and a trend toward improved clinical outcomes with sacubitril/valsartan compared to valsartan alone [16]. A prespecified participant-level pooled analysis of PARAGLIDE-HF and PARAGON-HF confirmed these cardiorenal benefits across the mildly reduced and preserved EF spectrum [17]. Additionally, sacubitril/valsartan improved quality of life metrics in patients with HFpEF [18].

### Safety, Tolerability, and Neurocognitive Safety
The safety profile of sacubitril/valsartan is generally favorable, though symptomatic hypotension is more common than with ACEi or ARB therapy [1, 12]. Importantly, because neprilysin is one of the enzymes that degrade amyloid-beta (Aβ) peptides in the brain, theoretical concerns were raised regarding the potential long-term risk of Alzheimer's disease or cognitive decline. However, a prespecified analysis of the PARAGON-HF trial evaluating cognitive function via the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) found no difference in cognitive decline between patients randomized to sacubitril/valsartan versus valsartan [19]. This neurocognitive safety was further confirmed in patients with HFrEF, showing no adverse signal and even potentially lower rates of neurocognitive diagnoses in real-world cohorts [20].

From a cardiorenal perspective, sacubitril/valsartan exhibits a preservation of renal function [21]. It is associated with a slower decline in estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and a lower risk of worsening renal function compared to enalapril or valsartan, even in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) [22, 23]. Furthermore, a post-hoc analysis of PARADIGM-HF demonstrated that sacubitril/valsartan significantly improved glycemic control (HbA1c) in patients with both HF and diabetes [24]. However, the drug is not recommended for acute myocardial infarction without pre-existing HF, as the PARADISE-MI trial did not show superiority over ramipril in preventing CV death or incident HF in the acute post-MI setting [25]. In pediatric populations, the PANORAMA-HF trial demonstrated that sacubitril/valsartan was well-tolerated and resulted in similar or greater reductions in NT-proBNP compared to enalapril in children with HF due to systemic left ventricular systolic dysfunction [26].

### Clinical Guidelines and Practical Considerations
Current clinical guidelines from the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) and the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association/Heart Failure Society of America (AHA/ACC/HFSA) reflect a strong consensus, designating sacubitril/valsartan with a Class I recommendation as a foundational pillar of guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) for patients with chronic HFrEF [27, 28, 29]. For patients with HFmrEF and HFpEF, guidelines offer a weaker, yet supportive (Class IIb or IIa) recommendation, particularly for those in the lower range of the ejection fraction spectrum [28, 29]. 

A critical safety mandate in clinical practice is the avoidance of concomitant ACEi therapy due to a significantly increased risk of angioedema [1, 30]. When switching from an ACEi to sacubitril/valsartan, a strict 36-hour washout period is required to allow complete clearance of the ACEi before ARNI initiation [27, 28, 30].

### Conclusion
Sacubitril/valsartan has fundamentally changed the management of heart failure. From chronic HFrEF to acute decompensated settings, and extending into the mildly reduced and preserved ejection fraction spectrum, neprilysin inhibition combined with angiotensin receptor blockade provides robust cardioprotective, renoprotective, and symptomatic benefits, making it an indispensable cornerstone of contemporary heart failure therapy.
